opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest change is that we've stopped trying to hand-engineer every piece of the robot's intelligence. For decades, robotics meant building a separate system for perception, one for planning, one for control, and then writing a lot of task-specific code to glue them together. That works well in a factory where the same part shows up in the same place every time. It falls apart the moment you ask the robot to do something slightly different.

What's changed is that foundation models have given us a general-purpose layer of understanding that we didn't have before. A vision-language model already knows what a mug is, what "put it next to the sink" means, and roughly how objects in a kitchen relate to each other. You don't have to teach the robot common sense from scratch anymore. That gets you a surprisingly long way on the high-level reasoning: figuring out what to do and in what order.

The second piece is that the learning recipes that worked for language are starting to work for actions. Transformers, diffusion policies, large-scale imitation learning: these let you train a single policy across many tasks and have it generalize, instead of training a narrow controller per task. And the techniques for collecting demonstration data, like teleoperation rigs and cheaper hardware, have improved enough that people can actually gather the kind of diverse data these models need.

That said, I'd be careful not to overstate where we are. The bottleneck has shifted to data. In language we had the whole internet. In robotics there's no equivalent corpus of physical interaction, so everyone is working out how to get it: teleoperation at scale, simulation, learning from human video. Reliability is the other big gap. A demo that works 80% of the time is exciting in a research setting, but in a real deployment you need something closer to 99.9%. Closing that last stretch is where a lot of the hard work is going to be over the next few years.

So the short version is that the "brain" got dramatically more general. Now the question is whether we can feed it enough real-world experience to make the "body" equally general.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the big change is really that the robotics problem has turned into a language-model problem, or at least a foundation-model problem. When I was working on robotics at OpenAI, we were doing the Rubik's Cube with the robot hand, and the thing that was so hard then was that you had to learn a policy essentially from scratch for every task. You'd do a ton of simulation, a ton of domain randomization, and at the end you'd have something that could solve one problem, and it wouldn't generalize to the next one. There was no shared understanding of the world underneath it.

What's changed is that now you have models that come in with a huge amount of prior knowledge. They understand what a cup is, what it means to put something in a drawer, what "gently" means. So instead of teaching a robot the entire world from zero through trial and error, you're really just teaching it the last mile of how to move its actuators to carry out intentions it already understands. And that's a much smaller problem.

The second piece is data. We've figured out that the recipe that worked for language, which is take an enormous amount of diverse data and a big model and let it generalize, also works for perception and increasingly for action. Teleoperation data, video, simulation, all of it can get pooled together in a way that wasn't possible when every lab had its own bespoke setup. And I'd add the hardware's gotten cheaper and more standardized, so you can actually collect that data at scale.

So I don't think it's one breakthrough. It's that the whole stack, the priors, the data, the hardware, finally lined up at the same time. And once you have general capability, the tasks you can attack go from one to many pretty quickly.

r003.rationale: It attributes broader robotic capability to foundation models’ prior knowledge and to the priors, data, and hardware coming together, describing the remaining problem as smaller and general capability emerging quickly.

astra-6.text:
I think the big change is that we’re moving from programming robots for individual tasks to teaching them through data. Traditionally, you could build a robot that did one thing very reliably, but adapting it to a new environment or a new task required a lot of engineering. Now, models can learn representations that transfer across tasks, so you’re not starting from scratch every time.

And language and vision models give you a much richer starting point. A robot needs to understand what it’s looking at and what you want it to do, as well as how to move. We’ve made a lot of progress on those first two pieces. The challenge is connecting that understanding to reliable physical actions, where the data is harder to collect and mistakes have real consequences.

r001.rationale: The response says language models help robots understand what people want, but does not state that LLM-based interfaces reduce the cost of specifying tasks.

r002.rationale: It mentions progress in language and vision models, but does not clearly identify integrating strong vision encoders with language-model intelligence as an enabler of general-purpose robotic tasks.

r003.rationale: The response mentions learning transferable representations, but does not attribute faster development to building on frontier models and an accumulated technology and research stack.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big change is that we’re moving from programming robots for individual tasks to training models that can generalize across tasks. Historically, you could make a robot do one thing very reliably, but every new task required a lot of engineering. In a messy environment, there are just too many situations to anticipate by hand.

With learning, the robot can start to connect what it sees with what it should do. And models that learn from images and language give you a much richer starting point: you don’t have to teach every concept entirely through robot demonstrations.

The challenge is still translating that understanding into reliable physical action. But if experience on one task helps with the next task, you get a very different path toward robots that can do a wider variety of things.
